Exclusivity is not guaranteed. SQS standard queues are at-least-once: 'more than one copy of a message might be delivered', even within the visibility timeout, and a message also returns to other consumers if it is not deleted in time. RabbitMQ also redelivers unacked messages to other consumers. For the lecture's non-idempotent total_blogs++ this means possible double counts.
precise_version: A message in a queue is normally handed to one consumer at a time (hidden by the visibility timeout / held unacked), but delivery is at-least-once: duplicates and redelivery to another consumer can happen, so consumers must be idempotent (or use an SQS FIFO queue with deduplication).

First half is right: Kafka docs: 'Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default.' But 'not truly exactly-once' undersells it: since 0.11 transactional producers plus read_committed consumers give exactly-once for read-process-write within Kafka (e.g. Kafka Streams). The real limit is external side effects (like a DB count++), which 'generally requires cooperation' from that system.
precise_version: Kafka is at-least-once by default. It offers real exactly-once processing for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines (transactions + read_committed); exactly-once effects on external systems (a DB update) need idempotent writes or storing offsets with the data.

Conflates two ideas. CRDTs are replicated data types that let replicas be updated independently and merged without coordination (distributed systems). 'Lock-free data structures' usually means single-machine concurrent structures built on atomic CAS (e.g. lock-free queues). Both avoid locks, but they are different families.
precise_version: Alternatives to locks include lock-free/atomic structures on one machine (CAS-based) and, across replicas, CRDTs: replicated data types that merge concurrent updates automatically without coordination.

A transaction alone does not prevent lost updates if the app reads the count, adds 1 in code and writes it back. Under PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED both transactions can read 100 and write 101. What works: an in-SQL atomic update (UPDATE ... SET claps = claps + 1, which applies to the latest row version), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE with retry.
precise_version: Use an atomic in-database update (SET claps = claps + 1) or lock the row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or a stricter isolation level with retries; wrapping a read-then-write in a default-isolation transaction is not enough.

precise_version: SQS standard queues are best-effort ordered and at-least-once; SQS FIFO queues keep per-message-group ordering and deduplicate, so per-entity ordering is possible on SQS too (with lower throughput per group).

Shard assignment is not done by the Kinesis service. The Kinesis Client Library (KCL) does it in your consumers, using a DynamoDB lease table so each shard is held by one worker at a time. With the raw API (GetShardIterator/GetRecords) you must name the shard yourself.
precise_version: With the KCL you don't pick shards: KCL workers coordinate shard leases through a DynamoDB table (billed to you). Using the low-level Kinesis API, you specify shards explicitly.

note: The reason is right in spirit: per-partition ordering plus a single-integer offset per partition per group makes tracking cheap. But it is a design choice, not a fundamental impossibility: Kafka share groups (production-ready in 4.2) let several consumers read one partition, tracking per-record state and giving up strict ordering.
precise_version: Classic consumer groups give each partition to one consumer so that Kafka keeps order and tracks progress with one offset per partition; share groups (KIP-932, Kafka 4.2) allow several consumers per partition by tracking per-record acknowledgements, without ordering guarantees.

Google Pub/Sub's ack deadline is a direct equivalent (default 10 s, 10 to 600 s per modify). RabbitMQ has no per-message visibility timeout: unacked messages are requeued when the consumer's channel/connection closes, and a consumer delivery-ack timeout (default 30 min) closes the channel.

Correct: SQS exposes no partitions. AWS does document that FIFO queues store data in internally managed partitions keyed by message group ID ('You don't manage partitions').

Plain durable/persistent queues are still destructive (a message is removed once acked), so they don't cover the stream use case. The feature that does is RabbitMQ Streams (since 3.9, 2021): an append-only log with non-destructive reads, many consumers and replay from an offset/timestamp.
precise_version: RabbitMQ covers the stream use case with RabbitMQ Streams (3.9+), an append-only replicated log that many consumers can read and replay; ordinary durable queues still delete messages once acknowledged.

No Kafka feature named 'broadcast' was found in the Apache Kafka docs/KIPs. Pub/sub fan-out (every consumer group gets every message) has always been Kafka's core model. The recent big change is share groups (queue semantics), not broadcast.
precise_version: Kafka has always supported pub/sub: each consumer group independently receives all messages of a topic. Recent releases added share groups (KIP-932) for queue-style consumption; there is no separate 'broadcast' feature.
